chapters.name: Chapter 1: Knowing and feeding your soil

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Reading your soil with your eyes and hands
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Do a simple field check of your soil and write down what it tells you.
This lesson builds toward: On one of your own fields, you will do a field check of colour, texture, worms, roots, water and plant signs and write down what it shows, treating plant signs as clues to confirm with a soil test.
You can learn a lot about soil with a spade, your hands and your eyes. Healthy soil is dark, crumbly and smells earthy. It has earthworms and other small creatures, roots go deep, and rain soaks in instead of running off. Poor soil is pale or hard, forms a crust after rain, cracks badly when dry, or stays wet and smelly.
Feel the texture: wet a small ball of soil and rub it between your fingers. Sandy soil feels gritty and falls apart; it drains fast and loses nutrients. Clay soil feels sticky and can be rolled into a long thin ribbon; it holds water and nutrients but can get waterlogged and hard. Loam is in between and is easiest to farm.
Look at the plants too. Yellow lower leaves on maize can mean too little nitrogen. Purple leaves on young maize can mean too little phosphorus. Weeds such as striga (witchweed) often show tired, low-fertility soil. These are clues, not proof: a soil test tells you for sure.
Step by step:
- Dig a hole about one spade deep in three places in the field.
- Look at colour, layers, roots and any hard layer.
- Count earthworms in one spadeful.
- Wet a ball of soil and feel it: gritty (sandy), sticky (clay) or in between (loam).
- After rain, note where water runs off or stands.
- Write what you found for each part of the field.
Words to know:
- Soil texture: how sandy, silty or clay-like a soil is; it decides how fast water drains.
- Loam: a soil with a good mix of sand, silt and clay.
- Hardpan: a hard layer under the surface that roots and water cannot get through.
- Striga: a parasitic weed (witchweed) that attacks maize, sorghum and millet, common on poor soils.
Try it now: Do the field check in one of your fields: dig in three places, feel the texture, count earthworms, and write one line for each spot. Take a phone photo of each hole so you can compare next season.
You can now check your soil in the field and describe its texture, life, drainage and warning signs.

check.q: What can yellow lower leaves on maize point to?
options: Too much water in the leaves
check.why: Yellow lower leaves on maize can mean too little nitrogen; a soil test confirms it.

check.q: After rain, your field forms a hard crust and the water runs off. What do you write in your field check?
options: A sign of poor soil, to confirm with a soil test
check.why: Crusting and runoff are signs of poor soil; a soil test tells you for sure what it needs.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Getting a soil test and taking a good sample
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Take a soil sample the right way and know where to send it for testing.
This lesson builds toward: For one field, you will take a soil sample the right way and name where to send it for testing, with many small samples mixed into one clean sample per part of the field.
A soil test tells you what your eyes cannot: how acidic the soil is (pH) and how much of the main nutrients it holds. Many soils in wetter parts of Kenya, Nigeria and Ghana are acidic, which locks nutrients away from the crop; a test tells you whether lime would help. Without a test, you may spend money on the wrong fertilizer.
Where to get a test: in Kenya, KALRO runs soil laboratories (for example its soil fertility laboratory at Kabete, Nairobi) and some counties have their own soil labs. In Ghana, the CSIR-Soil Research Institute at Kwadaso, Kumasi offers laboratory analysis. In Nigeria and elsewhere, ask your state or county extension office, agricultural university or research institute. Fees, lab locations and waiting times change, so call or check before you go.
KALRO's own guide says sampling is the biggest source of error in a soil test. One handful from one spot does not represent a field. Take many small samples across the field, mix them, and send one clean mixed sample for each field or each part that looks different.
Step by step:
- Choose one field (or one part that looks the same).
- Walk in a zigzag and take 10 to 20 small samples, top 15 to 20 cm, with a clean spade or auger.
- Avoid odd spots: old manure heaps, ash, paths, anthills, fertilizer bands.
- Mix all samples well in a clean bucket (not a fertilizer bag).
- Take about half a kilo of the mix, air-dry it in shade, and label it: name, field, date, crop planned.
- Take it to the lab before planting so results arrive in time.
Words to know:
- pH: a number that shows how acidic or alkaline soil is; most crops like it near neutral.
- Acidic soil: soil with a low pH that locks up nutrients such as phosphorus.
- Lime: a ground rock product that makes acidic soil less acidic.
- Composite sample: many small samples from one field mixed into one.
Official sources:
- Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO): contact for soil analysis
- KALRO: Guide for Soil Sampling and Pre-Treatment for Soil Fertility Evaluation
- CSIR-Soil Research Institute, Kwadaso, Kumasi (Ghana)
Try it now: Find the nearest place that tests soil: call your extension officer or check KALRO, CSIR-SRI or your state research institute. Write its name, fee and waiting time. Then mark on a sketch of your field the zigzag path you will walk to sample it.
You can now take a proper mixed soil sample and know where to get it tested.

check.q: What does soil pH tell you?
check.why: pH shows how acidic the soil is; acidic soil locks nutrients away and may need lime.

check.q: One part of your field is waterlogged and the rest is dry and sandy. How do you sample?
options: Mix the wet and dry parts into one sample
Send a separate mixed sample for each part that looks different
Sample only near the manure heap
check.why: Each field, or each part that looks different, gets its own clean mixed sample.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Building organic matter with compost and manure
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Make a compost heap and use manure safely to build soil organic matter.
This lesson builds toward: Using crop residues, green material and manure, you will make a compost heap and plan how to add organic matter, with no residues burned and no fresh manure on seedlings.
Organic matter is the dark, decayed remains of plants and animals in the soil. FAO calls it the key to drought-resistant soil: it holds water like a sponge, feeds earthworms and soil life, holds nutrients so rain does not wash them away, and makes soil crumbly so roots can grow.
You add organic matter by leaving crop residues on the field instead of burning them, by adding manure and compost, and by growing legumes and cover crops. Burning residues and ploughing again and again both use up organic matter.
Compost is easy to make: build a heap or pit with layers of dry material (maize stalks, dry grass), green material (fresh weeds, leaves, kitchen waste) and manure, with a little soil between layers. Keep it moist like a squeezed sponge, and turn it every two to three weeks. It is ready in about two to three months when it is dark, crumbly and smells like soil. Let fresh manure rot before use; fresh, hot manure can burn seedlings.
Step by step:
- Choose a shaded spot near the field and water.
- Lay a base of coarse stalks for air.
- Add layers: dry material, green material, manure, a little soil; repeat.
- Water each layer so it is moist, not soaking.
- Push a stick into the heap; if it is warm, it is working.
- Turn the heap every two to three weeks.
- Use when dark and crumbly, in planting holes or rows.
Words to know:
- Organic matter: decayed plant and animal material in soil that holds water and nutrients.
- Compost: rotted plant and animal waste used to feed the soil.
- Crop residues: stalks, leaves and husks left after harvest.
- Cover crop: a crop grown mainly to cover and feed the soil.
Official sources:
- FAO: The importance of soil organic matter (key to drought-resistant soil)
Try it now: Start a compost heap or pit this week with what you have: stalks, weeds, kitchen waste and manure. Write the date, the layers you used, and a reminder in your phone to turn it in two weeks.
You can now make compost, use manure safely, and explain how organic matter helps your soil.

check.q: What goes into a compost heap?
options: Layers of dry material, green material and manure, with a little soil between
check.why: Compost is built in layers of dry material, green material and manure, kept moist and turned.

check.q: After about three months your compost is dark, crumbly and smells like soil. What do you do?
options: Leave it for two more years
check.why: Compost is ready when it is dark, crumbly and smells like soil, after about two to three months.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Keeping soil healthy season after season

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Crop rotation and intercropping with legumes
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Plan a three-season rotation and a legume intercrop for one field.
This lesson builds toward: For one field, you will plan a three-season rotation and a legume intercrop, with a legume in the plan and spacing that lets both crops get light.
Growing the same crop on the same field every season drains the same nutrients and builds up its pests, diseases and weeds. Crop rotation means changing the crop on a field from season to season, for example maize, then beans or groundnut, then sorghum or cassava.
Legumes such as beans, cowpea, groundnut, soybean and pigeon pea work with bacteria in small lumps (nodules) on their roots to take nitrogen from the air. Some of that nitrogen stays in roots and leaves for the next crop, especially if you leave the residues on the field.
Intercropping means growing two crops together, such as maize with beans, sorghum with cowpea, or cassava with groundnut. It covers the soil, spreads risk, and can give more total food from the same land. Keep spacing that lets both crops get light, and plant the legume early enough to establish.
Step by step:
- List the fields you farm and what grew on each last season.
- Plan the next three seasons so no field has the same crop twice in a row.
- Put a legume in each field at least once in three seasons.
- Choose one intercrop pair, such as maize and beans.
- Leave legume residues on the field after harvest.
Words to know:
- Crop rotation: changing the crop grown on a field from one season to the next.
- Legume: a plant such as beans, cowpea or groundnut that can add nitrogen to the soil.
- Nodules: small lumps on legume roots where bacteria fix nitrogen from the air.
- Intercropping: growing two or more crops together on the same field.
Official sources:
- FAO: The importance of soil organic matter (key to drought-resistant soil)
Try it now: Draw a simple table: your fields down the side, the next three seasons across the top. Fill in a crop for each box so that every field gets a legume once and no field repeats a crop. Dig up one bean or groundnut plant and look for nodules on the roots.
You can now plan a crop rotation and a legume intercrop that feed your soil.

check.q: What are nodules on legume roots?
options: Small lumps where bacteria take nitrogen from the air
check.why: Legumes work with bacteria in root nodules to take nitrogen from the air.

check.q: You plant maize and beans together, but the beans get no light. What do you change?
options: Use spacing that lets both crops get light, and plant the beans early enough
check.why: Intercrops need spacing that lets both crops get light, with the legume planted early enough to establish.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Mulching and stopping erosion
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose and lay out mulch and simple erosion controls for a sloping field.
This lesson builds toward: For a sloping or bare field, you will choose mulch and erosion controls and lay them out along the contour, with the contour marked with help from extension where needed.
Bare soil is lost soil. Heavy rain knocks soil loose and runoff carries the richest top layer away. Mulch, a layer of crop residues, dry grass or leaves on the soil surface, softens the rain, keeps soil moist and cool, and feeds the soil as it rots. FAO notes that on slopes much more of the ground needs to be covered by residues to stop erosion than on flat land.
On slopes, work across the slope, never up and down it. Plant and ridge along the contour (a line at the same height across the slope). FAO describes contour ridges as a good method for smallholders with hand tools or oxen, and grass strips (for example Napier grass) along the contour as a cheap alternative to terraces; the grass can also feed livestock.
On steeper land, stone lines, contour bunds and bench terraces (such as fanya juu terraces in Kenya) hold soil and water. They take work to build and keep up, and lines laid out wrongly can make erosion worse, so ask your extension officer to help mark the contour.
Step by step:
- Walk the field after rain and mark where water runs and soil is washed.
- Mark contour lines across the slope with a simple A-frame or water-tube level, or with help from extension.
- Plant, ridge and weed along the contour lines.
- Plant grass strips or build stone lines or bunds along some contours.
- Cover the soil between rows with mulch.
- Check and repair after each heavy rain.
Words to know:
- Mulch: a layer of residues, grass or leaves spread on the soil surface.
- Erosion: soil being washed or blown away.
- Contour: a line across a slope where every point is at the same height.
- Terrace: a level step cut into a slope to hold soil and water.
Official sources:
- FAO: Rainfall runoff management techniques for erosion control
- FAO TECA/STI portal: Mechanical soil conservation strategies to reduce soil erosion
Try it now: After the next rain, walk your field and mark on a sketch where water runs and soil is washed. Choose one control (mulch, contour ridges, grass strip or stone line) for the worst spot and write when you will put it in.
You can now spot erosion on your farm and choose mulch and contour controls to stop it.

options: A line straight up the slope
A line at the same height across a slope
check.why: A contour is a line at the same height across the slope; ridges and grass strips follow it.

check.q: You want to build fanya juu terraces on a steep field. What do you do first?
options: Ask your extension officer to help mark the contour
Dig straight up and down the slope
check.why: Lines laid out wrongly can make erosion worse, so get help marking the contour.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Fertilizer basics: right source, rate, time and place
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a fertilizer plan for one crop using the 4Rs.
This lesson builds toward: For one crop, you will write a fertilizer plan using the right source, rate, time and place, with rates taken from a soil test or local recommendation.
Crops need nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P) and potassium (K), plus smaller amounts of other nutrients. Mineral fertilizer gives them quickly and in known amounts. The 4R idea, used in extension across Africa, helps you get the most from every bag: the right source, at the right rate, at the right time, in the right place.
Right source: the product that supplies what your soil test says is missing (for example a phosphorus fertilizer at planting, a nitrogen fertilizer for topdressing, and lime if the soil is acidic). Right rate: the amount your soil test and local recommendation give for your crop and target yield; more is not always better and wastes money. Right time: when the crop needs it, for example nitrogen topdressing on maize at about knee height, when the soil is moist. Right place: close to the roots, such as in the planting hole or a band beside the row, not touching the seed, and covered so rain does not wash it away.
Use fertilizer together with organic matter; the two work better than either alone. Buy sealed bags from registered agro-dealers and check the label. A phone AI assistant can help you understand a soil test report in plain words, but the rates come from the lab, your extension officer or the official recommendation for your area.
Step by step:
- Read your soil test or local recommendation for the crop.
- Source: write which product supplies each missing nutrient (and lime if needed).
- Rate: write the amount per acre or hectare that the recommendation gives.
- Time: mark planting and topdressing dates on your calendar.
- Place: plan to put it in the hole or band, not touching seed, and cover it.
- Buy sealed bags from a registered agro-dealer; keep the receipt.
Words to know:
- NPK: nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P) and potassium (K), the three main crop nutrients.
- 4Rs: right source, right rate, right time, right place for fertilizer.
- Topdressing: adding fertilizer, usually nitrogen, to a growing crop.
- Agro-dealer: a shop that sells seed, fertilizer and other farm inputs.
Official sources:
- 4R Plant Nutrient Management in African Agriculture: an extension handbook for fertilizer management
- Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO): contact for soil analysis
Try it now: Final task: write your one-page soil plan for one field. Include what your field check found, your soil test plan or results, how you will add organic matter, your rotation or intercrop, how you will stop erosion, and a fertilizer line for each nutrient: source, rate, time and place.
You can now use fertilizer by the 4Rs and put together a full one-season soil plan for your field.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Field check and soil test No field check, or no plan for a soil test. Field check results written down, with when and where a soil test will be taken, or what it said. Uses the soil test results to shape the rest of the plan. Organic matter No organic matter added, or residues burned. A plan to keep residues and add compost or rotted manure, with timing. Includes a compost heap already started on the farm. Rotation and legumes The same crop every season, with no legume. A three-season rotation or a legume intercrop with sensible spacing. Both a rotation and an intercrop, with residues left on the field. Cover and erosion Soil left bare, or working up and down the slope. Mulch or cover, and erosion controls along the contour where the field slopes. Names who will help mark the contour and how the controls will be kept up. Fertilizer by the 4Rs Fertilizer is listed with no rate source, timing or placement. Source, rate, time and place written for each product, with rates from a soil test or local recommendation. Combines fertilizer with organic matter and notes where the rate came from. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part of the plan and check it again.

check.q: What does "right source" mean in the 4Rs?
options: The cheapest bag in the shop
The bag with the brightest label
The product that supplies what your soil test says is missing
check.why: The right source supplies the nutrients your soil test says are missing.

check.q: A seller offers cheap fertilizer from an open sack with no label. What do you do?
options: Buy it because it is cheap
Buy sealed, labelled bags from a registered agro-dealer instead
Mix it with your own fertilizer
check.why: Buy sealed bags from registered agro-dealers and check the label.
